rv.q: It’s a rare musical that can warm your heart and chill you to the bone all at once – and that makes The Witches essential viewing for all but the most sensitive kids.
Theatre’s Roald Dahl adaptation ‘The Witches’ really is for everyone.
Kirkwood's script has an embarrassment of riches.

" I’ll admit that, perhaps because of the Olivier’s treacherous acoustics, I wasn’t able to catch every syllable of the quicksilver lyrics. If I’m being ultra-critical, I’d add that the mechanised mice were a tad slow. But don’t be put off: this is a stunning achievement.
This is the Christmas show to beat – a deliciously spiky supernatural tale that honours the dark streak in Roald Dahl’s child-pleasing writing.
This wickedly entertaining show will surely put a mischievous grin on anyone’s face.
Lyndsey Turner's production is a lavish, characterful family show that artfully blends the surprising and the familiar.
The good news is that this musical adaptation is true to Dahl's anarchic, grobblesquirting spirit.
The National’s show is sure to be a hit and I blame Dahl for my stubbornly ongoing reservations.
Dave Malloy’s songs (with lyrics by Malloy and Kirkwood) sound as if they are still in development, sometimes oddly tuneless and accompanied by thin piano notes or a stomping orchestra.
Fun enough for the festive season, but I can’t say I was fully bewitched.
It’s the best Dahl adaptation since Matilda, and the best new musical I’ve seen this year, hands down.
Lyndsey Turner's production combines exuberant fun, quick-witted comedy and a positive attitude towards death to produce an entralling, clever and incredibly funny production.
With such excellent production values and genuine heart behind performances, who cares?
It’s a deftly rendered production, a high-quality piece of family entertainment that skilfully blends the playful and the macabre, and does justice to the author’s distinct comic style.
There's something resolutely original and unashamedly fun about this latest Dahl musical makeover.
Using Dahl’s architecture, Kirkwood and Malloy have written a very witty and incredibly entertaining show, blending the silly with the scary to excellent effect.
Not a perfect show, it does at least have plenty of heart.

The risks taken by the makers of The Witches have certainly paid off. This show is darker, ruder, and funnier than Matilda, and though it may lack some of the polish of that megahit in this first run, I enjoyed it not one iota less.

For the parent generation add some dry witty lines and throwaway touches (the awful spoilt child is called Bruno dePfeffel Jenkins – ha!). Then add a magnificent song from the Grand High Witch about what a nuisance children actually are, “assholes!”, never giving you a quiet or private moment.
'The Witches' is a resounding success.

The creative sorcery of playwright Lucy Kirkwood and director Lyndsey Turner put the right mix of fright and fun into the cauldron to produce a near perfect family show, with sackfuls of inventive visuals, pacy action, and irreverent humour for children, while throwing a bone to the adults.
Brace yourself for the best family show since the National’s production of His Dark Materials.
The vibrancy of the design matches the powerful music which is consistently upbeat and gives us more than one earworm to hum on the way home.

At this point I thought the National might have a colossal Matilda-sized hit on its hands, but then I found myself utterly perplexed, because when they reach Bournemouth something happens that I would never have predicted: the musical becomes boring.
When it works – usually when Rigby and Triplett are onstage – The Witches is a dark broomstick ride of delight to enchant all the family this Christmas.

cn.t: Critics largely embrace this darkly funny musical adaptation, praising Lucy Kirkwood's witty script and strong performances, though some find it overlong. Most agree it's the best Dahl adaptation since Matilda, balancing scares with humor.
